expr: (list (progn (string-match "foo" "Foo bar") (replace-match "baz qux" nil t "Foo bar")) (progn (string-match "foo" "FOO bar") (replace-match "baz qux" nil t "FOO bar")) (progn (string-match "foo" "Foo bar") (replace-match "bAz" nil t "Foo bar")) (progn (string-match "f" "F") (replace-match "xy" nil t "F")))
note: WHAT FIXEDCASE nil ACTUALLY DOES, measured rather than read off the docstring, because two of these four are not what `capitalise the replacement' suggests. Emacs answers ("Baz Qux bar" "BAZ QUX bar" "BAz bar" "XY"). Element by element: a capitalised match capitalises EVERY WORD of a multi-word replacement, not just the first; an upcased match upcases the whole of it; the capitalising rule is `upcase-initials' and not `capitalize', so `bAz' becomes `BAz' and keeps the interior capital that `capitalize' would have flattened; and a ONE-CHARACTER uppercase match `F' counts as UPCASED rather than capitalised, so a two-character replacement comes back `XY' and not `Xy'. kg declined it, in writing, which is what this case asked for: `replace-match' accepts FIXEDCASE and ignores it, as `replace-regexp-in-string' already did, so one argument means one thing across the family. And the case turns out to be UNASKABLE as well as declinable: every element matches "foo" or "f" against an upper-cased subject, which needs `case-fold-search' to match at all, so kg answers the `replace-match subexpression does not exist' error of an empty register rather than a string. An implementation of the case rule would have been surface no row in this corpus could check.
